q: Lafite Rothschild and Latour both lie in which commune?
exp: Pauillac holds three of the five First Growths, more than any other commune, and its wines are the Medoc benchmark for structure and cassis.

q: Margaux and Haut-Brion are two of the five First Growths. Where are the other three?
exp: Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild are all Pauillac, which is why that commune is treated as the Medoc benchmark.

q: Travelling north through the Medoc, which of the four great communes comes last?
exp: Running north the order is Margaux, Saint-Julien, Pauillac, Saint-Estephe. The northernmost has more clay and a firmer, sterner reputation.

q: Pessac-Leognan was carved out of which larger appellation?
exp: Created in 1987 for the northern, finest part of Graves, it holds Haut-Brion and the best dry whites of Bordeaux.

q: Immediately south of Pauillac lies which commune?
exp: Saint-Julien sits between Pauillac and Margaux, and is often described as balancing Pauillac's power with Margaux's finesse.

q: Margaux is most often praised for which stylistic quality?
exp: Margaux's lighter, more gravelly soils give the most aromatic and silken of the great Medoc communes, though it is also the largest and most varied.

q: Gravel dominates the Left Bank. Why does that suit Cabernet Sauvignon?
opts: It holds water for the whole season
It drains freely and stores daytime heat
It raises acidity in the fruit
exp: Deep gravel banks shed water and radiate stored heat, which is what lets a late-ripening variety finish in a maritime climate.

q: The four classified communes of the Medoc all sit within which broader appellation?
exp: Haut-Medoc covers the southern, finer half of the peninsula. The plain Medoc appellation covers the northern part beyond it.

q: Chateau Petrus is found in which appellation?
exp: Petrus sits on Pomerol's clay plateau and is made almost entirely from Merlot. Pomerol is tiny and has no classification at all.

q: Among major Bordeaux appellations, Pomerol is unusual in lacking what?
exp: Pomerol has never been classified. Reputation and price do the ranking instead, which has not held its best estates back.

q: Pomerol, Fronsac and Lalande-de-Pomerol are all small. Which Right Bank neighbour dwarfs them?
exp: Saint-Emilion dwarfs its neighbours in area and number of estates, which is part of why it needs a classification and Pomerol does not.

q: Montagne-Saint-Emilion is an example of what?
exp: The satellites, including Montagne, Lussac, Puisseguin and Saint-Georges, may append the Saint-Emilion name to their own.

q: Fronsac lies close to which river?
exp: Fronsac and Canon-Fronsac sit just west of Saint-Emilion above the Dordogne, and are long regarded as offering Right Bank character at lower prices.

q: Cotes de Bourg and Blaye face the Medoc from which side?
exp: Both look across the Gironde at the Medoc from the Right Bank, and both are Merlot-led.

q: Pomerol's plateau is known for a distinctive soil feature. What is it?
exp: A band of iron-bearing clay, the crasse de fer, underlies the best of the plateau, and is commonly credited with the density and the mineral, truffled note of the wines.

q: How often is the Saint-Emilion classification revised?
exp: Periodic revision is the point of it: estates can be promoted or demoted, which makes it the living counterpart to the fixed 1855 list.
